title: Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen correlations between mechanical oscillators revealed through SU(1,1) interferometry
authors: Max-Emanuel Kern, Stefano Marti, Raquel Garcia-Belles, Andraz Omahen, Igor Kladaric, Arianne Brooks, Yiwen Chu, Matteo Fadel
abstract: Quantum correlations are essential for achieving quantum advantage in computing, communication and sensing. Moreover, their observation challenges and constrains our fundamental understanding of nature. Mechanical oscillators in the quantum regime provide an appealing platform for preparing and investigating quantum correlations at macroscopic scales. Despite substantial progress, however, continuous-variable quantum correlations stronger than entanglement have not yet been observed in this macroscopic regime. Here, we report the experimental observation of continuous-variable Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen correlations between two spatially-separated mechanical oscillators with an effective mass of $\sim 16 \,μg$ each. This is achieved by coupling them to a superconducting qubit which allows for engineering a two-mode squeezing interaction when parametrically driven. Crucially, we show that this interaction can be used to witness quantum correlations through the realization of a mechanical SU(1,1) interferometer. Our results expand the toolbox of operations in circuit quantum acoustodynamics and demonstrate that quantum correlations stronger than entanglement can also be observed in macroscopic systems, thereby shedding light on the boundary between quantum and classical regimes.
summary: The researchers experimentally demonstrated continuous-variable Einstein–Podolsky–Rosen correlations between two macroscopically separated mechanical oscillators. They achieved this by coupling the resonators to a superconducting qubit and engineering a Two-Mode Squeezing (TMS) interaction, which functions as the core element of an SU(1,1) interferometer. This work confirms that quantum correlations stronger than entanglement can be observed in large-scale physical systems.
main_problem: To experimentally observe continuous-variable Einstein–Podolsky–Rosen (EPR) correlations between two spatially-separated mechanical oscillators, which are quantum correlations stronger than entanglement.
main_result: The experiment successfully observed these continuous-variable EPR correlations by realizing a mechanical SU(1,1) interferometer using engineered Two-Mode Squeezing (TMS) interactions. This demonstrates that macroscopic systems can exhibit quantum correlations beyond simple entanglement.
method: The study employs parametric driving to engineer the TMS interaction between two high-overtone bulk acoustic wave resonators coupled via a superconducting qubit. Quantum correlations are then witnessed by implementing an SU(1,1) interferometer sequence.
model_or_system: The platform is a circuit quantum acoustodynamics (cQAD) device featuring two HBARs coupled to a transmon qubit. The dynamics are modeled using Hamiltonians that allow for the generation of effective Two-Mode Squeezing (TMS) interactions, which replace traditional beam splitters in the interferometer.

important_parameters: Effective mass ($\sim 16 \, \mu	ext{g}$), coupling strengths ($g_a, g_b$), parametric drive strength, and the time duration of the squeezing operations.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the engineered TMS interaction accurately models the required quantum operation for the interferometer. Theoretical predictions for the TMS rate showed minor deviations from measurement.
figures_summary: Figures detail the device micrograph and spectroscopy confirming non-overlapping phonon modes, followed by characterization of the TMS rate dependence on drive strength, and finally showing interference fringes and the minimum value of the EPR steering criterion $E(\phi)$ vs. phase $\phi$.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the physical platform (cQAD) and the goal of observing strong quantum correlations. It then details the characterization of the key interaction (TMS rate calibration). Finally, it applies this calibrated interaction to build and test the mechanical SU(1,1) interferometer to witness EPR steering.
why_interesting: This work bridges macroscopic quantum mechanics with fundamental quantum information protocols by using mechanical oscillators as a robust platform for continuous-variable entanglement witnesses. It expands the operational toolbox in cQAD systems.
